statement: A **2-tangle diagram** is a regular diagram in a disk of two properly embedded tangle arcs and possibly finitely many closed tangle components, with four specified endpoints on the disk boundary; the arcs and circles are disjoint in the represented 3-ball, while their projections may have crossings. A **flyping circle** is a simple closed curve in the projection sphere whose intersection with the diagram consists of exactly three points, exactly one of which is a crossing; the circle is transverse to both branches at that crossing and to the diagram at the other two points. A small annular neighborhood of this circle has two complementary tangle disks. A **flype** fixes the tangle in one disk, interchanges which pair of strands crosses in the annular neighborhood, and turns over the tangle in the other disk: its projected tangle is reflected and all its over-under crossing data are reversed. This turnover is a half-turn in three-dimensional space about an axis in the projection sphere. Component orientations are transported by this motion, and the exterior diagram is fixed. The move with the opposite choice of fixed disk is also allowed; a disk containing no crossings is allowed. A flype whose fixed tangle has no crossings is called an **entire flype**. Diagrams are drawn on the oriented projection sphere; a **sphere planar isotopy** is an orientation-preserving smooth isotopy of that sphere carrying the decorated diagram. A plane diagram is obtained by choosing a point of the sphere outside the projection and deleting it. At each crossing of a link diagram, a **crossing ball** is a small 3-ball in which the overpass lies on the upper hemisphere and the underpass lies on the lower hemisphere, with the rest of the link outside that ball. Replacing all crossing disks by upper hemispheres or by lower hemispheres gives the shifted projection spheres $S_+$ and $S_-$. A **saddle disk** in a crossing ball is a properly embedded disk whose boundary meets each of the two hemispheres in two arcs and whose interior passes across the equatorial crossing disk. For a closed embedded surface transverse to the link and to $S_+$ and $S_-$, each component $C$ of its intersection with either shifted sphere has a **bubble word**: read once around $C$, recording $P$ each time it crosses the link and $S$ each time it passes through a crossing ball along a saddle disk. The surface is in **bubble standard position** if every such word is nonempty and no word records the same crossing ball more than once. A **Conway sphere** is an embedded sphere meeting the link transversely in four points; it is in crossing-ball standard position when its intersection with the crossing balls consists of saddle disks and its shifted-sphere intersection curves satisfy the bubble-standard conditions.

statement: Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

Let $K_8$ be the standard figure-eight knot, presented as the boundary of the square plumbing of one positive and one negative Hopf band, with one boundary component. A positive Hopf band is an oriented annulus whose positive normal push-off of its core has linking number $+1$ with the core; a negative Hopf band has linking number $-1$. A square plumbing identifies a square in the boundary collars of the annuli with the four boundary edges alternating between the annuli, then smooths corners. With the twist convention that the positive twist $R_a$ sends $a\mapsto a$, $b\mapsto a+b$, and the negative twist $L_b$ sends $a\mapsto a+b$, $b\mapsto b$, the monodromy is $R_a\circ L_b$. After capping $\partial F$ by a disk, its action on the ordered homology basis $([a],[b])$ is represented by $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

statement: Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be an embedded link smooth except at finitely many planar corners. Supply disjoint coordinate boxes about these corners, each meeting $K$ in one arc lying in a coordinate plane, with its two oriented one-sided tangents in a common open half-plane. Fix one positive graph coordinate in each box. A rounding means replacement there by a smooth planar graph in that coordinate, agreeing with the old arc near the box ends. Then arbitrarily small such roundings exist, equal to $K$ outside these boxes. Any two sufficiently fine such roundings are related by a smooth ambient isotopy supported in those same boxes, fixing their exterior pointwise. Component labels and orientations are retained. Consequently every surface disjoint from the boxes stays fixed; for a two-point decomposing sphere disjoint from the boxes, triviality or nontriviality of its side tangles is unchanged when one such rounding is replaced by another.

statement: Assume countable choice. A bridge diagram is a smooth regular oriented planar link diagram whose height function has only nondegenerate critical points, with distinct critical and crossing heights, and with neither crossing preimage a height-critical point. A planar isotopy between two bridge diagrams, stationary near its ends, can be changed arbitrarily little through regular planar diagrams, relative to those ends, so that it has finitely many exceptional times. At each such time exactly one of the following happens: a birth or death of two height-critical points; a crossing passes through a nondegenerate height-critical point of one of its branches; or two distinct special points exchange height order, where a special point is a maximum, a minimum, or a crossing. Away from these times the diagrams are bridge diagrams. The diagram orientations, crossing decorations, and planar isotopy class are retained throughout.
